tour.title: Memorials, Parks & the Skyline: CKS to Elephant Mountain
tour.summary: The modern city end to end: a strongman's marble memorial, a food street born of exile, the green lung in the middle of everything, the world's tallest tower of its decade, and a forest staircase to the postcard skyline at sunset.
tour.overviewText:
Taipei in January wears a raincoat. The light is grey, the pavements are wet, and the drizzle comes at you sideways off the hills — and the hills are the point. Taipei sits in a basin, a former lake bed drained by the Tamsui River on its way to the sea, ringed by green ridges you can see from almost any street. This walk uses the whole bowl: it starts at the marble monument a defeated government built to its founder, crosses a food street and the city's great central park, walks into the glass towers of the new downtown, and finishes on a stone staircase above the rooftops, watching the lights come on.

First, who governs here, because the flags and signs are confusing. Taiwan's official name is the Republic of China; Beijing claims the island as a province of the People's Republic of China; most residents favour the status quo of neither unification nor formal independence. The government you are about to meet — Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang — lost the Chinese Civil War on the mainland in 1949, crossed the strait, and ruled Taiwan under martial law until 1987. Chiang had led that government from 1928; on this island he ruled as president for twenty-six years, until his death in 1975. Supporters credit him with land reform, an economic take-off and keeping Beijing out. Critics blame him for the February 28 Incident of 1947, when troops crushed an island-wide uprising, and for the White Terror that followed, in which an estimated tens of thousands were imprisoned, killed or disappeared — figures historians still argue about. What is not argued about is the ending. Taiwan lifted martial law in 1987, held its first direct presidential election in 1996, and has since swapped ruling party peacefully several times. That transition is the thing this walk keeps running into.

After that, the city. Taipei's money is no longer factories but what factories became: this is where the island's finance, media, design and government sit, while the chip plants that pay for much of it are an hour south. Its daily life runs on food, convenience stores and the metro, and on a winter weekday the people around you will be office workers on a lunch break, students cutting class, and pensioners doing slow tai chi in the rain.

The walk is about seven kilometres, mostly flat, and takes a long half-day. It begins at the memorial in Zhongzheng, moves east through the food lanes of Yongkang and the trees of Da'an, crosses into the planned skyscraper district of Xinyi, and climbs the sandstone hill at the basin's edge for the sunset view the whole island photographs.

Practicals. January in Taipei is cool and damp, roughly 14 to 19 degrees, so bring a rain shell rather than an umbrella for the ridge, and shoes with grip — the hill's stone steps are polished and slick when wet. The memorial, the park and the trail are free; the tower's observation deck charges, in New Taiwan dollars. Start around 11.30 so you are on the ridge for the light. Hours and prices move; verify at the gate.

Go hungry, go early, and save your legs for the last staircase.
tour.difficulty: Easy, then genuinely steep. About six and a half kilometres of level city pavements, lanes and park paths, then a stone staircase up Xiangshan (Elephant Mountain): 183 metres of climb over roughly 1.5 kilometres, with between six hundred and seven hundred steps. There is nowhere flat to rest in the first stretch, the steps are uneven and slippery after rain, and you will come back down them in the dark.
tour.bestTimeOfDay: Start around 11.30 on a weekday. The memorial is open by nine, Yongkang is quieter before the lunch queue, and the timing lines up with the one fixed appointment on this walk: in mid-January the sun sets in Taipei at about 17.20 and the light is gone by 17.45. Aim to be on the ridge by 17.00. Read the tower's observation deck as optional — if you go up it, keep it to an hour, because the hill is the better show. The memorial, the street and the park are open daily; the only thing a hard rain cancels is the honour guard drill.

stops.name: Chiang Kai-shek Memorial Hall
stops.narration:
Eighty-nine white steps climb to this hall, one for every year Chiang Kai-shek lived. That number tells you what kind of building this is: a monument that measures a man.

Chiang was born in Zhejiang province in 1887 and led the Nationalist Party, the Kuomintang, from 1928. He fought the Japanese, lost a civil war to Mao Zedong's Communists, and in 1949 moved his government — the Republic of China — to Taiwan, where he ruled as president until his death in 1975. Under him the island lived under martial law from 1949 to 1987, then the longest such period in the world. Supporters credit him with land reform, an economic boom and keeping Beijing out. Critics blame him for the February 28 Incident of 1947, when troops put down an island-wide uprising, and for the White Terror that followed, in which an estimated tens of thousands were imprisoned, killed or vanished — figures still disputed.

Hence the argument carved into the site. In 2007 this was renamed the National Taiwan Democracy Memorial Hall and the gate inscribed Liberty Square; in 2009 the next government restored Chiang's name and left the square's. A 2017 transitional justice law ordered authoritarian symbols to be removed or reframed, and the hall is becoming a democracy-education park, closed each 28 February. Since July 2024 the honour guards no longer stand beside the statue: the drill happens outside, hourly from nine to five, and is cancelled in rain.

Go in. The bronze statue is 6.3 metres tall, the hall 76 metres, and the blue octagonal roof nods to the number eight, which Chinese culture links to good fortune. Then turn around: the best thing here happened after Chiang died. In March 1990, twenty-two thousand students sat down in this square demanding direct presidential elections. They got them, in 1996.

The hall is free and open daily to 6pm, closed 28 February; verify at the gate.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free entry to the hall, the exhibition halls and the park. No ticket and no booking; the observation is only that prices and hours at sites like this move, so check the board at the gate, and note the drill is cancelled when it rains.
stops.openingHours: Hall roughly 09:00 to 18:00 daily, closed Lunar New Year's Eve and Day, 28 February, and maintenance days. The park is open about 05:00 to 24:00. Honour guard drill hourly from 09:00 to 17:00 on Democracy Boulevard, weather permitting. Confirm on the day.
stops.accessibility: The park and the lower level are step-free, with lifts inside the hall and level paths across the square. The main hall is reached by two flights of 89 steps, though there is a lift route from the ground floor for anyone who needs it. Ask at the information desk.
stops.insiderTip: Skip the statue and head down to the lower level: the permanent exhibition on Taiwan's martial-law years and the island's route to democracy is the honest counterweight to everything upstairs. Then walk the length of the square to the Liberty Square gate and read the inscription from the outside.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the south gate, the Gate of Great Piety, cross Aiguo East Road and walk east along it for about six hundred metres, then turn south into Yongkang Street and follow it down past Yongkang Park. It is about 1.1 kilometres, fifteen minutes on foot, flat and largely shaded by old camphor trees.

stops.name: Yongkang Street
stops.narration:
Read the street names before you read the menu. Yongkang, the lane you are standing on, plus Lishui and Jinhua beside it, are all towns in Zhejiang province on the mainland: in 1947 the post-war government renamed great swathes of Taipei after places across the strait, and this quiet grid kept its mainland addresses. Before that, under Japanese colonial rule, the neighbourhood was Shōwa-chō, an era name that survives on a small antiques market further down.

Now eat: everyone else is. Beef noodle soup — niu rou mian — is the island's unofficial national dish, and it is a dish of exile rather than tradition. Cattle here were plough animals and beef was rarely eaten; the staple starch was rice, not wheat. Both habits changed after 1949, when roughly two million soldiers and civilians followed Chiang's defeated government across the strait. Veterans from Sichuan and northern China opened noodle stalls to make a living, and American wheat aid through the 1950s made flour suddenly cheap. Simmered beef shank, soy sauce, star anise and pickled mustard greens over wheat noodles: refugee food that turned into the national comfort bowl. Yongkang Beef Noodles has served it on this street since the 1960s.

Then the dumplings. In 1958 a couple called Bing-Yi Yang and Pen-Mei Lai opened a cooking-oil shop on the corner of Xinyi Road; in 1972 they started steaming xiaolongbao — paper-thin dumplings holding pork and jellied stock that melts into soup — and the oil business quietly lost the argument. That shop became Din Tai Fung, now a chain across a dozen countries, and the corner still carries the queue to prove it.

Prices are in New Taiwan dollars, NT$ for short. A bowl of beef noodles runs a few hundred NT$, dumplings rather more, and the queue outside is the most reliable review in the city. Hours posted on the door are a wish, not a promise.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Nothing to pay to walk the street. Food is the expense: a bowl of beef noodles is a few hundred NT$, a tray of soup dumplings rather more. Check the menu board before ordering and carry some cash for the small stalls.
stops.openingHours: The street is public and open at all hours, but shops and restaurants cluster around lunch, roughly 11:30 to 14:00, and dinner from about 17:30. Individual restaurants close one weekday each and the famous ones close when they sell out. Verify at each door.
stops.accessibility: Level pavements and a narrow lane shared with scooters, delivery vans and parked cars. Doorways mostly have a step or a raised threshold, and the older noodle shops are cramped inside with fixed stools. Manageable, not step-free.
stops.insiderTip: Walk the whole street south to Yongkang Park before choosing where to eat: the alley behind the main drag holds the small counters with the shortest menus and the longest local queues, and the park is where everyone takes the food they could not finish.
stops.nextStopDirections: Walk south along Yongkang Street to its end, then turn right into Jinhua Street and left onto Xinsheng South Road, crossing at the lights. The trees ahead are the park. It is about 900 metres, twelve to fifteen minutes, and you enter Da'an Forest Park from its western side.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: MAm ROFOW 022, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Da'an Forest Park
stops.narration:
Twenty-six hectares of trees in the middle of a city of millions: locals call Da'an Forest Park the lungs of Taipei, and on a wet January afternoon you can have most of it to yourself.

It is younger than it looks. The Japanese colonial government set this land aside as parkland in 1932 — Park Number Seven — but the park was not built for another sixty years. In the meantime the ground filled with military dependents' villages and an informal settlement of people with no title to it. After a long legal fight, the city cleared the site in 1992, evicting around twelve thousand residents, and opened the park on 29 March 1994. It opened before the facilities were finished, and Taipei nicknamed it Mud Park. The canopy that gives it the name took thirty years to grow.

Two things are worth knowing. First, the statue near the southern edge is Guanyin, the Buddhist goddess of compassion, carved in 1985, and it is here under a compromise of its own: the evicted residents wanted it gone, Buddhist leaders defended it, and the city settled by keeping it as public art rather than a place of worship — no incense, no offerings. Second, the park appears on the city's list of disaster-prevention parks: the assembly point for this neighbourhood if a major earthquake hits. In a basin of narrow lanes and tall buildings, open ground is emergency infrastructure, and knowing where yours is counts as local knowledge.

Walk the loop. Look for egrets stalking the ecological pond and turtles stacked on the logs, and note that the benches are full by six in the morning with people doing tai chi — this is the neighbourhood's living room, which is exactly what it was built to be. Free, open all year, with a metro station at the north-west corner and a car park under the lawns.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public park, open all year, no ticket. The occasional festival on the lawns is free too, though ice cream and coffee carts charge what they charge.
stops.openingHours: Open daily, all year, at all hours; the paths are lit and used from early morning until late evening. Best in daylight. Verify locally if a festival or a typhoon closure is on.
stops.accessibility: The most accessible stop on the walk: wide paved paths, gentle gradients, benches, step-free entrances from every side and a lift-equipped metro station at the north-west corner. The ecological pond has low edges and no barriers, so watch small children.
stops.insiderTip: Find the Guanyin statue on the southern side and read the story of the settlement that stood here: the park is a monument to a demolition as much as to greenery, and almost nobody walking past the tai chi crowds knows it.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave the park on its eastern side and follow Xinyi Road east for just over three kilometres, with the tower in front of you the whole way: about forty-five minutes on foot, along wide sidewalks, past the residential blocks of Da'an and into the glass canyons of Xinyi. If the drizzle has set in, ride instead — Da'an Park station and Taipei 101 station are three stops apart on the red Tamsui–Xinyi line, about six minutes underground.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: 玄史生, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Taipei 101
stops.narration:
Look straight up. That is 508 metres to the tip of the spire — 101 floors above ground, five below — and from its opening on New Year's Eve 2004 until the Burj Khalifa took the title in 2010 it was the tallest building in the world.

The tower rises in eight sections of eight floors, each flaring outward like a stalk of bamboo, and eight is the number Chinese culture ties to prosperity. The floor count is a deliberate one-better-than-perfect: one hundred is the traditional number of completion, so 101 means the new century, and — since 1/01 is 1 January — all the years to come.

The engineering is the part to remember. This is typhoon and earthquake coast, so the tower is built for winds of sixty metres a second — 216 kilometres an hour — and the strongest quake expected in 2,500 years, standing on 380 concrete piles driven up to eighty metres into bedrock. Flexibility does half the work, and a tuned mass damper does the quiet rest: a steel ball weighing 660 tonnes and 5.5 metres across, made of 41 welded plates and hung on cables from the 92nd floor down to the 88th. When the tower sways one way the ball swings the other and cancels up to forty per cent of the motion. You can see it from the 88th floor. In 2015 Typhoon Soudelor pushed it a record one metre.

Tickets: the 89th-floor deck is NT$600, the 101st floor adds about NT$380, and the outdoor Skyline 460 skywalk at the top is NT$3,000; hours are roughly 10am to 9pm daily. All of it moves — verify at the counter. The lift from the 5th to the 89th floor takes 37 seconds, the fastest in the world when it opened. Go up if the cloud allows, then come down: the next stop gives you the same city from a hill.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Observation deck about NT$600 per adult for the 89th floor; the 101st-floor top deck around NT$980 combined and the outdoor Skyline 460 skywalk about NT$3,000. Rates and inclusions are revised often — verify at the ticket counter, and note the outdoor deck closes in bad weather.
stops.openingHours: Observation deck roughly 10:00 to 21:00 daily, last entry around 20:15, with occasional closures for weather or maintenance. The mall below keeps longer and different hours. Verify on the day.
stops.accessibility: Fully step-free: lifts to the deck, level floors, wide doors and accessible toilets throughout. Queues at peak times are the real obstacle, and the fast lift changes pressure, which some ears complain about.
stops.insiderTip: Go up around 40 minutes before you plan to leave and take the 91st-floor outdoor terrace as well as the 89th: the open air is the difference between a photograph through glass and one without it. Then ask the lift attendant to point out the damper on the 88th floor on the way down.
stops.nextStopDirections: Leave by the Xinyi Road side and follow the signs south-east through the Xinyi district; it is about 1.2 kilometres to the trailhead, fifteen to twenty minutes on foot. You pass the department stores, cross Songshou Road and reach Xiangshan metro station — the trail entrance is beyond it, up the lane beside the small Lingyun temple. You are at the foot of the steps.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: AngMoKio, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Xiangshan Trailhead
stops.narration:
Stop and look at the stairs. That is the Xiangshan trail — Elephant Mountain — and it begins with a staircase that climbs and does not stop climbing.

You are at the western trailhead, beside a small neighbourhood temple, Daitiandian Lingyun. The route gains 183 metres in about a kilometre and a half of stone steps — people count somewhere between six hundred and seven hundred of them — through low forest to a ridge of viewpoints. There are several platforms on the way, and you do not have to reach the summit to get the view; the first proper one is fifteen minutes up.

This hill is one of the Four Beasts — Elephant, Lion, Leopard and Tiger — the sandstone ridge forming the south-eastern rim of the Taipei basin. Taiwan is a young island being squeezed upward where two tectonic plates collide, which is why it has the earthquakes, the steep crumbly hills, and the tower you just left, whose damper exists because of exactly this geology. The rock under your feet is soft young sandstone, and the tree ferns leaning over the steps are an ancient plant lineage that was already old before flowering plants existed.

Practicals, honestly. The trail is free and open at all hours, and there is nothing to buy on the hill, so pick up water at the convenience stores near the metro station before you start. From Taipei 101 it is fifteen to twenty minutes on foot to this trailhead; the metro station behind you is the terminus of the red Tamsui–Xinyi line. Allow twenty to thirty minutes for the climb, and expect to be breathing hard: the first stretch is the steepest and has nowhere flat to stop. Wear shoes with grip, because in January drizzle these steps are wet and polished. And bring a light, because you will be coming back down them in the dark.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free public trail, no gate and no ticket. There is nothing to buy on the hill; the last shops and the metro station are at the bottom.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours, every day. Most people climb in daylight or for sunset; there is limited lighting on the upper steps, so a torch matters if you are descending after dark.
stops.accessibility: Steep stone steps with handrails on one side only in places, uneven rises, exposed tree roots and slick surfaces after rain. Not suitable for wheelchairs, and hard going with a stroller or for anyone unsteady on stairs. There are benches shaped like elephants on the way up.
stops.insiderTip: Fill your water bottle and use the toilet at the bottom, because there is neither on the hill. Then pace the first staircase slowly — the people who sprint the first hundred steps are the ones sitting on the ledge five minutes later.
stops.nextStopDirections: Take the steps up. Keep left at the first junction and follow the signs for the Six Giant Rocks; the path climbs through the trees for fifteen minutes to the first lookout platform and then continues about ten minutes more along the ridge to the boulders. It is short and steep — take it slowly and step aside for people coming down.
stops.photoAttribution: Photograph: dennis, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Xiangshan Ridge Viewpoint (Six Giant Rocks)
stops.narration:
Below you the Taipei basin is laid out like a diagram: the flat floor of a former lake bed, the Keelung River curling north, a ring of green ridges on every side, and Taipei 101 standing directly in front of you, close enough to look almost small.

Watch the next twenty minutes: the window people climb for. In mid-January the sun drops at about 17.20 and the last light is gone by 17.45, and the tower switches on while the sky is still pale — the city lit, the sky not yet black. The notches in the boulders are there so visitors can scramble up and stand, in the photograph, as tall as the skyscraper.

Then turn the walk over in your head, because it was never about the view. You started in a marble hall built by a one-party state to its founder, with a bronze statue 6.3 metres tall and eighty-nine steps up to it. You ate the exile food that became a national dish, on a street named for a town across the strait. You crossed a park that was a squatters' village until 1992. You walked into a planned downtown of glass. And you climbed a sandstone hill that was forest long before any of it. Taiwan's argument with its own past — how much of Chiang Kai-shek belongs in a public square, what martial-law cost, what this island is called — is not settled. You have just walked several sides of it in seven kilometres.

Two last things. The descent: wet steps, no daylight, handrail and torch — this mountain collects sprained ankles every week. Be a good guest: this is a neighbourhood path locals run before work, so do not plant a tripod across the stairs.

Then follow the steps down to Xiangshan station, about fifteen minutes, and ride the red line home — trains run until around midnight. Go and eat something else.
stops.entranceFeeNote: Free viewpoint, no ticket. The only costs are the metro home and whatever you eat afterwards.
stops.openingHours: Open at all hours. Come for the hour before sunset, roughly 16:30 to 17:45 in January, and stay for the first forty minutes of the city lights. Lighting on the upper steps is sparse.
stops.accessibility: Not accessible. Reached only by the stone staircase, and the last section to the boulders involves rocky ground and short scrambles. Handrails exist on parts of the route but not all of it. The lower platforms are easier and give nearly the same view.
stops.insiderTip: Stay twenty minutes past sunset rather than leaving with the crowd: the sky goes deep blue behind a lit tower, and the steps are far less crowded going down once the photographers have packed up. Keep your phone charged for the torch.
stops.nextStopDirections: End of the walk. Follow the steps back down to Xiangshan station — about fifteen minutes, and much easier than the climb — and take the red Tamsui–Xinyi line north to Taipei 101, Da'an Park or Taipei Main Station. Trains run until around midnight; check the last departure at the station. If you still have appetite, the food streets of Yongkang are five stops and a short walk away, and are open late.
